subject: Incorporating a random effect to zero-inflated negative binomial regression

messages.author: 7f2609deedcb09b0
messages.subject: Incorporating a random effect to zero-inflated negative binomial regression
parts:
I'm hoping to incorporate a random effect into a zero-inflated negative binomial model. I am modeling the count of officer-involved shootings by race and body-camera status for each county, so I have six rows for each county: white/body-camera, white/no camera, hispanic/body camera, etc. Most of the counts are zero, and obviously I want to account for the fact that the six rows per county are not independent of each other. I was told that I should be able to fit this model in Stan, but I don't have much experience in Stan. 

Through the manual, I found the following elements: 

#### random effect
parameters {
  real theta[J];      #per-trial treatment effect
  real mu;            #mean treatment effect
  real<lower=0> tau;  #deviation of treatment effects
}
model {
  y ~ normal(theta, sigma);
  theta ~ normal(mu, tau);
  mu ~ normal(0, 10);
  tau ~ cauchy(0, 5);
}


### zero-inflated model (Poisson)
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> y[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
  real<lower=0> lambda;
}
model {
  for (n in 1:N) {
    if (y[n] == 0)
      target += log_sum_exp(bernoulli_lpmf(1 | theta),
                            bernoulli_lpmf(0 | theta)
                            + poisson_lpmf(y[n] | lambda));
      else
        target += bernoulli_lpmf(0 | theta)
        + poisson_lpmf(y[n] | lambda);
  }
}


How might I incorporate these two things together? Thank you for any advice you can offer.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Incorporating a random effect to zero-inflated negative binomial regression
parts:
You just need to write down the parameters and density
of the model you want to fit. Here's where you get
the zero inflated Poisson:

> target += log_sum_exp(bernoulli_lpmf(1 | theta),
> bernoulli_lpmf(0 | theta)
> + poisson_lpmf(y[n] | lambda));

so you could just replace that poisson with a negative binomial
and you get a zero inflated negative binomial.

Then any regression coefficients go into a model for the mean
and/or overdispersion just as they would in any other model.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Incorporating a random effect to zero-inflated negative binomial regression
parts: You might want to use the brms R package for this purpose. The package creates and fits the Stan model under the hood and so you don't have to worry about writing the Stan code yourself. It supports many response distributions among other zero-inflated negative binomial models.

parts:
Thank you for recommending this package. It looks quite useful. 

To include an offset and a random ("group") effect in a zero-inflated negative-binomial model, is the below a correct model call? In the example, I want to indicate that all of the fixed ("population level") effects are assumed to vary with the levels of the grouping factor groupVar. 

Also, how do I include an offset or exposure variable in this model? Should I add it in as a fixed effect? Is this what the parameter logm1 is used for?
 

fit_zinb1 <- brm(count ~ (persons + child + camper | groupVar), 
                 data = zinb, family = zero_inflated_negbinomial())
